analysis.one_liner: Bans military use of toxic PFAS firefighting foam by 2029 and directs a cleanup study.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Armed Services Committee and its Readiness subcommittee with no cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Defense Department to stop using firefighting foam that contains PFAS, the long-lasting 'forever chemicals' that have contaminated drinking water around military bases nationwide, by January 1, 2029. It also ordered a study of the best and cheapest ways to clean up PFAS-contaminated ground, with a report to the Armed Services Committees. It never left the House Armed Services Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Military families and people living near bases, whose drinking water has been contaminated by PFAS foam used in training at military installations, along with service members who train with the foam. A congressionally directed phase-out would also give water utilities and states a clearer path to forcing cleanup of contaminated sites.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Defense Department to use only non-fluorinated firefighting foam, free of PFAS, no later than January 1, 2029 [S2][S3].
Directs a study of best practices, costs, and timelines for cleaning up PFAS-contaminated ground, excluding incineration, with a report to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Defense Department budgets, and ultimately taxpayers, bear the cost of replacing foam and remediating contaminated sites; manufacturers of fluorinated foam and the PFAS chemicals inside it lose a major government customer.

drawbacks.text: The ten-year deadline (January 1, 2029) gives the military and foam makers a long runway, so contamination from continued use would continue for years [S3].
The bill only orders a study of cleanup methods and sets no cleanup standard or funding, so contaminated communities get information rather than remediation [S3].

Replacing fluorinated foam across military facilities carries real costs, and fluorine-free alternatives historically have raised performance questions for fuel fires, which is why the transition was given a long lead time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, achievable health measure: phasing out PFAS foam at military installations would directly cut a major source of drinking-water contamination for surrounding communities, though the slow timeline and study-only approach to cleanup limit how much it would accomplish. The main cost is budgeted replacement of foam and eventual cleanup, which is unavoidable either way.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee and then to its Readiness subcommittee, was never brought up for a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Kim introduced the bill on June 12, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Armed Services [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Readiness, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of PFAS and fluorinated firefighting foam kept their Defense Department business, and the military continued using the foam; families near contaminated bases gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS and foam makers kept their contracts

for.name: Rep. Andy Kim
for.role: Sponsor, House Armed Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring a Pentagon phase-out of PFAS firefighting foam

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on and no votes were ever recorded, so the partisan shape of the bill never took form [S4][S5].

industries.industry: PFAS chemical manufacturers (e.g. makers of fluorinated firefighting foam)
industries.note: The bill would have cut off military purchases of fluorinated foam, a core market for the chemicals, while the foam continues to contaminate drinking water around bases where ordinary families live.
DOD would bear foam-replacement and cleanup costs, but PFAS contamination also imposes health and liability costs on the military and the public that the phase-out would eventually reduce.
A congressionally directed study of PFAS cleanup practices would have fed into remediation work that these firms perform.
